paragraph: Section 14 opens the notes dated 27 February 1983 by returning to the letter to Quillen, especially (L, p. 1). Grothendieck describes homotopical algebra through spaces of maps and successive homotopies, then examines the formulation of isotopy, stratified structures, tubular neighborhoods, and the problem of wildness. His examples bring topoi and protopoi into the discussion and lead to the criticism of piecewise linear structures on p. 2, where the handwritten replacement R-valued specifies the functions under consideration. Section 15 takes up the resulting search for a formulation of homotopy types through localization. The local revisions on pp. 1–2 replace functions by maps, restrict suited to directly suited, and replace numerical by R-valued. The witness omits the typed maps after between such on p. 1, prints pretopoi where the scan reads protopoi, and retains numerical while omitting R-valued on p. 2; these readings are recorded as D01323, D01333, D01340, and D01341.

Section 15 reviews the descriptions of homotopy types through topological spaces, semi-simplicial sets, and cubical complexes, using localization as their common organizing construction. It recalls Kan complexes and the correspondence between chain complexes and semi-simplicial abelian groups, then places the stacks of the Quillen letter beside these descriptions through their homotopy groups. On p. 3 Grothendieck twice changes description to computation when discussing cohomology; the witness retains the deleted words (D01355–D01358). The dated 3.5 marginal note on p. 4 retracts the preceding claim about difficulty in extracting cohomology: it refers to using only the source and target structure of the stack, part of its primitive structure. Close inspection corrects the initial transcription at precisely these nouns. The witness expands this short note into a long discussion of hemispherical complexes, the globe category, and later sections 31, 34, and 90; that expansion exceeds the text visible in this margin (D01388). Section 16 resumes from this account with stacks over topoi and the motivation from noncommutative cohomological algebra.

Section 16 gives the motivation for stacks over a topos from noncommutative cohomological algebra, starting with Giraud’s treatment of H^i for i = 0, 1, 2 and extending the hierarchy of sheaves, 1-stacks, and higher stacks. It draws on the descriptions of homotopy types in section 15, and recalls the 1975 letters to Breen and Mme Raynaud’s thesis in discussing Lefschetz comparisons and cohomological depth. The language of coefficients and integration on p. 5 is developed through sections on the final object and the comparison with R Gamma F_*; p. 6 then fixes the infinite-order use of stacks and Gr-stacks and states the intended synthesis with homotopical algebra. On p. 4 the witness reads K^i where the scan has H^i (D01397); on p. 5 it loses the F in R Gamma F_* and substitutes j for the handwritten star after F (D01418, D01421). The inserted non commutative qualification on p. 5 is also absent from the witness (D01416). The next section continues the survey through categories as models.

The section renumbered 16-prime surveys the homotopy type associated with a small category through its presheaf topos and its nerve. It recalls Verdier’s construction and Artin–Mazur pro-homotopy types, then records Quillen’s correction of Grothendieck’s earlier restriction to sums of K(pi,1) spaces. The attempted argument through the left adjoint N-prime to the nerve contains the claim about K to NN-prime(K); the dated 5.3 margin on p. 7 explicitly calls this false and points to section 24, pp. 21–22. Page 8 asks about a closed model structure and adds the (!9) call; the scan carries an exclamation mark, corrected from the initial transcription’s 19. Page 9 returns to the coherators of the Quillen letter and to universal algebra as a way to organize the growing family of structures. The witness expands the short retraction on p. 7 into a footnote (D01467); the checked text preserves the visible short note. These pages supply the questions pursued in the later discussion of modelizers and test categories.

Section 17 adds the Artin–Mazur cohomological characterization to the preceding discussion of stacks as a unifying concept. Grothendieck explicitly refers back to section 15, and describes the role of twisted coefficients on the target space, including the noncommutative H^0 and H^1 terms. He relates this observation to obtaining homotopy information from étale cohomology of schemes and then examines its effect on the motivation for higher noncommutative cohomological algebra. The handwritten parenthesis on p. 9 reads namely, unification; the witness reads messy unification (D01507). The scan also retains say in the parenthetical ordinary homotopy types say (D01508), cancels that after however (D01512), and has their observation (D01513). The following section returns from this motivation to explicit corrections of the letter to Quillen.

Section 18, dated 28 February, collects corrections to the letter to Quillen before the itinerary of section 19. On p. 10 Grothendieck revisits fiber products in C-infinity, amalgamated sums in the dual category B-infinity, the passage from C_n to C_(n+1), intersections of maximal subcells, and the formulation of associativity beyond primary composition. He explicitly retracts the earlier blanket statement about binary amalgamated sums and replaces the proposed relation for secondary composition by a discussion of a square of homotopies. The margin drawing gives three regions f, f-prime, f-double-prime between poles s,t, with f intersect f-double-prime = {s,t}; the checked transcription restores this figure and equation from an incorrect AI prose placeholder, while the witness supplies only a description (D01540). The scan writes L to K and M to K after the displayed K amalgamated-over-L M; those written directions remain in the text. Page 11 introduces the names left and right coherators, then reads Bénabou’s bicategories in relation to 2-stacks and the geometric motivation of the Breen letters. The witness omits the phrase explaining topological intuition as support for understanding an algebraic formalism (D01560). Section 19 takes these corrections and the left/right terminology as the starting points of its program.
